n: In this lesson we shall examine mechanical asphyxia in six sections. The first section covers the concept and classification of hypoxia and asphyxia. The second studies the course of asphyxia, its stages and the postasphyxial state. The third presents the general external and internal signs. The fourth section is devoted to strangulation asphyxia: hanging, and strangulation by ligature and by hands. The fifth section deals with obturation asphyxia and drowning, that is, obstruction, water and diatoms. The sixth analyses compression and the effect of carbon dioxide in a closed environment.

t: Section 1: hypoxia and asphyxia in brief
n: The first section: hypoxia and asphyxia. Mechanical asphyxia is the term for a state in which a mechanical factor has impaired external respiration. Asphyxia proceeds with acute oxygen deficiency and a rise in carbon dioxide. The Greek meaning of the term is absence of pulse. Mechanical asphyxia is divided into three types: compression, obstruction and closed environment. That is, we first study the concept, then the three types. Remember: careful examination of the scene is of great importance here.

Types of hypoxia. Hypoxia is exogenous or endogenous. In exogenous hypoxia there are three forms: hypoxic, in which the air contains little oxygen; hyperoxic, in which oxygen is plentiful and acts over a long period; and hypercapnic, in which there is a lot of CO₂ in a closed environment. Endogenous hypoxia includes the respiratory type, that is, related to the lungs and airways. There are also the haemic, circulatory and cytotoxic types. Physiological hypoxia is temporary and occurs on exertion.

Classification of mechanical asphyxia. In the forensic medical classification three types of mechanical asphyxia are distinguished. The first is from compression: if the neck is compressed it is called strangulation asphyxia, if the chest and abdomen are compressed, compression asphyxia. The second is from obstruction: here the respiratory openings or airways are obstructed, and drowning also belongs to this group. The third is asphyxia occurring in a confined space. This classification serves as the basis for the following sections.

Autoerotic asphyxia, that is, sexual asphyxia. Here arousal arises against a background of hypoxia and hypercapnia. This state is more common in solitary middle-aged men. A ligature or a polythene bag is used as the method. Control is exercised with the hands, feet and special devices. At the scene, imitations, clothing of the opposite sex and pictures may be found. Careful examination of the scene is therefore important.

t: Section 2: course of asphyxia in brief
n: The second section: the course of asphyxia. Five stages are distinguished in the asphyxial period. Overall, the course begins with the pre-asphyxial period, followed by the asphyxial period. The duration of the stages is conventional and approximate. The postasphyxial state is seen when asphyxia does not end in death. The mechanism of death is related to cerebral hypoxia and cardiac arrest. In this section we shall examine in detail the stages of the asphyxial period, their signs and the postasphyxial state.

Duration of the stages of asphyxia. The main point on the slide is that the pre-asphyxial period lasts on average 20–30 seconds. This is the very beginning of the course of asphyxia. After it the asphyxial period begins, and its stages with their signs are shown on the next slide.

t: Stages of the asphyxial period: signs
n: The stages of the asphyxial period follow one another in sequence. The first stage is inspiratory dyspnoea: breathing quickens, and consciousness is lost within 40–60 s. The second is expiratory dyspnoea: clonic convulsions are seen, and urine and faeces are discharged. The third is a brief pause in breathing: breathing stops and the muscles relax. The fourth is terminal breathing: there is infrequent, irregular breathing, and the mouth opens. The last is complete cessation: paralysis of the respiratory centre occurs, while the heart beats for a further 3–10 minutes.

Reflex cardiac arrest. Death may also occur from cardiac arrest. Here receptors are stimulated: those of the carotid sinus, larynx, trachea and bronchi. As a result the heart stops reflexly. The general asphyxial signs have no time to develop. In such a case they may therefore not be found on the body. Remember: absence of signs does not exclude asphyxia.

t: Limitations in describing the course of asphyxia
n: Limitations in describing the course of asphyxia. It is necessary to know that the stages and their duration are conventional and approximate. They are based on analysis of observations of incomplete asphyxia. The only experiment was carried out by Minovici in 1905: hanging, on himself. In addition, the course depends on the type of action, its intensity and the state of health. That is, even under identical conditions the result may differ.

The postasphyxial state consists of four periods; they follow one another in Table 5.3. The first is asphyxial coma: atony, no reflexes, then convulsions appear. The second is stupor: consciousness is restored, first sopor, then drowsiness. The third is disorientation: confabulation and retrograde amnesia are seen. The fourth is residual effects; in mild cases they disappear without trace within 1–2 weeks.

The internal organs in the postasphyxial state. Hypoxia impairs the function of internal organs. Oedema develops in the lungs, and in the first hours this is regarded as an unfavourable sign. Dystrophy and focal necrobiosis arise in the liver. Changes characteristic of shock are found in the kidney. In the gastrointestinal tract erosions and ulcers form on the mucosa. In the cardiovascular system, with hypoxia of more than 3 minutes, persistent hypotension is seen.

The third section: general signs. General signs are not specific to mechanical asphyxia, that is, they are found regardless of the type of asphyxia. The reason is that they also occur in other types of rapid death. In assessment, therefore, the set of signs is taken into account. However, some are regarded as relatively pathognomonic: the asphyxial heart, anaemia and a contracted spleen. We shall study the external and internal signs separately.

The external general asphyxial signs are related to dyspnoea and convulsions. Cyanosis of the face and neck arises from convulsions during dyspnoea, but is not persistent. Extensive cadaveric lividity forms because the blood is fluid and saturated with carbon dioxide. Subconjunctival ecchymoses appear because of the sharp change in pressure during dyspnoea. Mydriasis is inconstant and depends on the action of catecholamines. Involuntary discharge of urine and faeces is explained by contraction of smooth muscle during convulsions.

The internal general asphyxial signs are likewise not specific individually. The blood is fluid and dark red, because there is hypercapnia and fibrinogenase activity rises. In the asphyxial heart the right chambers are fuller than the left. Venous congestion is related to hypertension of the pulmonary circulation. Tardieu spots are 2–3 mm, dark red, and lie beneath the pleura and epicardium. Anaemia and a contracted spleen indicate release of blood from the depots; this is Sabinsky's sign.

t: Diagnostic value of the general signs
n: Diagnostic value of the general signs. These signs also occur in other types of rapid death. For example, in sudden death from heart disease, electrical injury and anaphylactic shock. They are therefore not specific, and only the set is assessed. Three signs are regarded as relatively pathognomonic: the asphyxial heart, anaemia and a contracted spleen. This means that a conclusion cannot be drawn relying on a single sign.

The fourth section: strangulation asphyxia, that is, compression of the neck organs. This type accounts for more than 2/3 of deaths from mechanical asphyxia. The commonest is hanging: 65–70%. The main sign is the ligature furrow. Types: hanging, and strangulation by ligature, by hands, by a blunt object, and positional asphyxia. We shall study the signs of each type in turn.

Types of strangulation asphyxia. Compression of the neck is grouped by the compressing force. In the first group the compressing force is body weight: this is hanging, in which the ligature is tightened by body weight. In the second group an external force acts: strangulation by ligature, by hands and by a blunt object. Here ligature strangulation occurs under the action of another's force. The third group is positional asphyxia with the head flexed.

Hanging accounts for 65–70% of deaths from asphyxia. In most cases it is a method of suicide. Hanging is of two kinds. In typical, that is, complete hanging the body hangs freely in the ligature. In atypical, that is, incomplete hanging part of the body has support. The person may then be standing, sitting or lying. The difference lies in how much of the body weight falls on the ligature.

Ligature and knot. The knot is of particular importance from the criminalistic point of view. The ligature material may be soft, semi-rigid or rigid. By turns, a single-turn, double-turn or multiple-turn ligature is distinguished. The loop is sliding or non-sliding. The position of the knot is posterior if typical, anterior or lateral if atypical. When removing the ligature, it is cut on the side opposite the knot.

Factors of death in hanging. Several factors are significant together in death. The first is narrowing of the airway: the base of the tongue is displaced towards the pharyngeal wall. The second is impaired venous outflow, because the jugular veins are compressed. The third is cerebral circulation: intracranial pressure rises and brain activity is impaired. The fourth is reflex cardiac arrest, in which the vagus nerve and the sinocarotid node are compressed. With an atypical knot, vomiting and aspiration of material are also possible.

Classification of the ligature furrow. The furrow has the appearance of an abrasion. In incomplete asphyxia, with a semi-rigid ligature, it persists for 10–15 days. By site and direction the furrow is typical or atypical, oblique or horizontal. By turns it is single or multiple, and the ends are closed or open. By width it is wide or narrow, by depth superficial or deep. The relief is smooth or uneven, the consistency soft or hard.

t: Furrow: typical, atypical and universal ligature
n: The furrow appears different in typical hanging, atypical hanging and with a universal ligature. In general the furrow is more pronounced on the side opposite the knot. In typical hanging the furrow lies in the upper part of the neck, above the hyoid bone, in an obliquely vertical direction. In atypical hanging it lies in a lower part of the neck, and verticality decreases. With a universal ligature a furrow with closed ends forms, and a mark of the knot may remain.

t: Ligature material and appearance of the furrow
n: Ligature material and appearance of the furrow. The appearance of the furrow depends on the ligature material. With rigid material the furrow is denser and deeper, and is clearly seen on the side opposite the knot. With soft material the furrow is not clearly visible on the skin, even if the ligature is applied over soft material. On internal examination a whitish band is found in the projection of the furrow. This is called the "copper wire sign" and is associated with the name of Casper.

t: Internal signs of the eyes and neck in hanging
n: The internal signs of the eyes and neck in hanging depend on the site and force of the ligature. In anisocoria the pupil is wider on the side of stronger compression. Injury of the hyoid bone and cartilage is not characteristic of hanging, and is possible only if the ligature is low. Brouardel's sign is manifested by haemorrhage behind the pharynx and in the posterior wall. That is, the presence or absence of these signs depends on where and with what force the ligature acted.

t: Signs of neck stretching in hanging
n: In hanging, along with compression, the neck is stretched. Signs of stretching are seen mainly in obese persons in typical hanging with a jerk. Amussat's sign is a transverse tear of the intima of the carotid artery. Martin's sign is haemorrhage in the outer coat of the carotid artery. Walcher's sign is haemorrhage at the lower end of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Simon's sign is haemorrhage into the intervertebral discs of the neck. Remember: these signs show that the neck was stretched.

t: Establishing the vitality of the furrow
n: Establishing the vitality of the furrow. Under the microscope Neyding showed circulatory disturbance, and Kasyanov signs of reactive inflammation. The method is as follows: first a skin flap is taken from the area of the furrow. Then it is cleared of subcutaneous fat. Then it is examined in the light between two glass slides. If congestion is found in the ridge, this indicates vitality. That is, it can be established that the furrow was formed during life.

Hanging and ligature strangulation. Their mechanism is similar, but the signs differ. In hanging the compressing force is body weight, in ligature strangulation another's force. Hanging is commoner in suicide, ligature strangulation in homicide. In hanging the furrow is oblique and lies high, in strangulation horizontal and at the level of the cartilage. Signs of stretching may be present in hanging, and do not form in strangulation. Cyanosis and cadaveric lividity are less marked in hanging, more marked in strangulation.

Manual strangulation: the external marks are usually a sign of homicide. Finger marks are round or oval bruises. Nail marks are crescentic abrasions on the bruise. In strangulation from the front with two hands there is 1 mark on the anterior surface and 2–4 on the posterior surface on each side. In strangulation from behind with two hands, 2–4 marks are found on the anterior surface and 1 on the posterior surface on each side. If strangled over a soft object, there are few external injuries or none at all.

t: Manual and blunt-object strangulation: internal signs
n: In manual strangulation the internal injuries are more pronounced than the external. The horns of the hyoid bone are fractured, and the thyroid cartilage is fractured. Haemorrhage occurs in the soft tissues. In this case reflex cardiac arrest is commoner. In strangulation with a blunt object, for example a stick, the marks lie in the projection of the acting surface: bruise, abrasion and haemorrhage. Injury of the hyoid bone and cartilage is also possible.

Positional asphyxia. Here the head remains in a flexed position for a long time. This is often seen in unconscious persons or those unaware of themselves. Externally there is no ligature furrow on the neck. Internally a whitish band is found in the projection of the fold. The hyoid bone and larynx are not injured. Diagnosis rests on the circumstances of the event, and other causes are excluded.

t: Section 5: obturation and drowning in brief
n: The fifth section: obturation and drowning. In obturation the respiratory openings or passages are obstructed. If the openings are obstructed and there was no resistance, there are no characteristic signs. If the passages are obstructed, a foreign body or substance is found in the airway. Drowning is the term for obstruction of the passages by liquid. To establish vitality, diatoms and other laboratory methods are used. We shall go through these in turn.

Obstruction of the respiratory openings. In homicide, young children and the debilitated are more often victims. If there was no resistance, only general asphyxial signs are found, and no characteristic signs are identified. With resistance there are bruises and abrasions around the mouth and nose, haemorrhage in the oral mucosa, and injuries on other parts of the body. When covered with a soft object, fibres of the material are found in the mouth and nose, sometimes in the upper airways as well.

Obstruction of the airways. Impeded passage of air is the leading factor in death. Foreign bodies include a fruit stone, button, bone and dental prosthesis. Powdery substances are sand, soil, cement, grain and flour. Among liquids, blood and vomit may obstruct the passages. Predisposing factors are intoxication and head injury. In the reflex mechanism, spasm of the vocal cords and cardiac arrest occur.

t: Vomit in the airways: what it means
n: Finding vomit in the airways does not always mean obturation. In obturation asphyxia aspiration reaches the small bronchi and alveoli, the mucosa is congested and oedematous, and the acidic material damages the mucosa. In other cases, for example in resuscitation and cardiac massage, transport of the body or putrefaction, the material is scanty and is not found in the small bronchi. That is, the depth of spread of the material gives an important distinction.

Types of drowning. Drowning takes second place after hanging, with more than 300 thousand deaths a year worldwide. Three types are distinguished. True drowning is called aspiration, or "wet": water reaches the alveoli. Asphyxial drowning is spastic, or "dry": because of laryngospasm water does not enter the trachea and bronchi. The third is mixed drowning. Determining the type sets the direction of further examinations.

When do true and asphyxial drowning occur? The type depends on the circumstances and the state of the victim. True drowning is commoner in the warm season, in warm water and in persons who are intoxicated. Asphyxial drowning occurs under severe psycho-emotional stress, low water temperature and in young children. This means that knowledge of the circumstances helps to suggest the type.

Signs of drowning in the airways and lungs. General asphyxial signs may be present in both types. In true drowning the foam is persistent, white, later pink; in asphyxial drowning scanty, unstable and white. In the airways, in true drowning there is water and foreign matter; in asphyxial drowning they are not found. The lungs in true drowning are doughy and enlarged, in asphyxial drowning there is marked emphysema and the cut surface is dry. Beneath the pleura, in true drowning there are Rasskazov-Lukomsky-Paltauf spots, in asphyxial drowning only Tardieu spots. Haemodilution is present in true drowning, absent in asphyxial.

t: True drowning: blood and fluid signs
n: Blood and fluid signs in true drowning. Water passes into the blood through the alveoli. Cadaveric lividity is more often of pink and reddish shades. Casper's sign: the blood of the left heart is paler than that on the right. In the endocardium of the left chambers there is a reddish tint, that is, imbibition. Moro's sign: about 100 ml of fluid in the abdominal cavity. Fegerlund's sign: up to 300 ml of water in the stomach.

Drowning in sea water. The osmotic pressure of salt water is higher than that of blood, so the process runs differently. In true drowning in general, water passes from the alveoli into the blood, haemodilution and osmotic haemolysis occur, and Rasskazov-Lukomsky-Paltauf spots are present. In sea water, however, the fluid part of the blood passes into the alveoli and electrolytes pass into the blood. Hypovolaemia develops and the blood thickens. Rasskazov-Lukomsky-Paltauf spots are absent, and in some cases there is pulmonary oedema.

Air embolism in asphyxial drowning. First, marked emphysema develops. The alveolar septa are damaged. Air passes into the pulmonary veins. As a result air embolism forms in the left heart. To detect it the Sunsov test is used: the left ventricle is punctured. The test was first proposed by Sveshnikov and Isaev in 1986.

Additional signs of asphyxial drowning. Laryngospasm more often lets water into the stomach. Lymphohaemia is the finding of blood elements in the thoracic duct. Fegerlund's sign here is up to 1 l of water in the stomach. Sveshnikov's sign is 5–15 ml of fluid in the cavity of the base of the skull. Ulrich-Rostoshinsky's sign consists of haemorrhage in the middle and inner ear.

Sudden death in water. Immediately on entering the water the heart and breathing stop reflexly. The signs of asphyxia have no time to develop. Predisposing factors: heat stroke, extreme fatigue, a full stomach and intoxication. On examination a change leading to sudden death is found in the heart. Remember: in such a case absence of signs of asphyxia is to be expected.

Vitality: diatom plankton. A diatom is a single-celled aquatic plant with a siliceous shell. The particles are usually 15–50 µm, sometimes 200 µm. In true drowning water passes into the blood. Diatoms are carried with the blood and reach the organs through the systemic circulation. They are found in the parenchymatous organs and bone marrow. This finding therefore shows that the person breathed before death.

t: Diatom finding: where it is reliable
n: Where is a diatom finding reliable? The plankton must match the plankton of the water body. Diatoms in the parenchymatous organs and bone marrow are a sign of vitality and must necessarily match the water of the water body. In lung tissue they have no diagnostic significance, because they are found also when the body enters the water after death. In asphyxial drowning diatoms may be absent from the organs; the fluid of the base of the skull is then examined.

Other laboratory methods of establishing vitality. Special laboratory examinations are also carried out. Pseudoplankton consists of sand and plant dust, which are distinguished by polarising microscopy. In bacteriological examination Pseudomonas putida and P. fluorescens are found. In the blood-properties method the blood of the left and right heart is compared. These methods supplement the diatom examination.

Stay in water: skin changes. These changes are important for establishing the time. Within several hours the fingers and toes turn pale and wrinkle. At 2–5 days the "washerwoman's hand" appears on the palm. At 5–8 days on the soles, then it spreads to the backs of the hands and feet. At 10–15 days hair is easily pulled out. At 2–3 weeks the skin with the nails separates in the form of a "glove of death".

t: Influences on changes from a stay in water
n: Influences on the changes from a stay in water. These changes do not depend on the cause of death. If the water temperature is high, the changes proceed faster. Clothing, gloves and footwear slow the skin changes. In adults the epidermis is thick and prone to maceration. In newborns vernix caseosa protects. In the long term adipocere, that is, saponification, may develop.

t: Section 6: compression and closed environment in brief
n: The sixth section: compression and closed environment. Compression asphyxia is compression of the chest and abdomen. Its causes are disasters and crushing in a crowd. The characteristic sign is the ecchymotic mask, also called the Olivier-Danger mask. In a closed environment oxygen decreases and carbon dioxide rises. On the body, however, there are no changes characteristic of a closed environment.

Compression asphyxia: cause and danger. Intensity depends on force, site, direction and duration. Causes: natural disasters, that is, earthquakes and landslides; man-made disasters, that is, collapse of a building and overturning of a vehicle. In a crowd, in disorderly movement, for example in a stadium, crushing occurs. Frontal compression is more dangerous than lateral. Only with compression of the abdomen is the body relatively more tolerant.

Characteristic signs of compression asphyxia. Characteristic changes are added to the general asphyxial signs. The ecchymotic mask is manifested by swelling, bluish discolouration and haemorrhages of the face. Its site is the face, neck, upper chest and conjunctiva. The cause is impaired blood flow in the superior vena cava. In prolonged compression there is "carmine oedema", that is, the lungs are bright red. The apex and edge of the lungs are light pink and airy, that is, in a state of emphysema.

Carbon dioxide in a confined closed environment. The leading factor is the rise in carbon dioxide. At a concentration of 0.5% breathing quickens and ventilation increases. In children at 2.0–2.5% a danger to life arises. In adults death usually occurs at 8–10%. That is, the higher the concentration, the stronger the effect.

t: Confined closed environment: situations and signs
n: Confined closed environment: situations and signs. A completely closed environment includes earthquakes and landslides, a submarine and a refrigerator, children in an airtight chest, and also a plastic bag over the head. Incompletely closed ones include a deep well, silage pit, vegetable store, wine vessels and a fuel system; here toxins of fermentation and putrefaction also play a role. The body shows only general asphyxial signs and signs of rapid death, and no characteristic changes are observed.

t: Training case 1: furrow on the neck
n: Training case one. This is a hypothetical case, not a real examination. Given: a horizontal, continuous furrow on the neck. The furrow lies at the level of the thyroid cartilage. The hyoid bone is intact. The signs of Amussat and Walcher are absent. There are two questions: hanging or ligature strangulation, and which signs indicate this. Think the answer through yourself.

Answer to the first case. The set of signs is consistent with ligature strangulation. The reason is that the furrow is horizontal, continuous and at the level of the cartilage. Injury of the hyoid bone and signs of stretching do not occur in such a case. In addition, injuries of struggle and self-defence are examined. That is, the conclusion rests not on one sign but on the set.

Training case two. This too is a hypothetical case; not a real examination. Given: white foam around the mouth and nose, the lungs doughy and enlarged. Beneath the pleura there are large pink spots, and the blood of the left heart is paler. Questions: which type of drowning, and how is vitality confirmed.

Answer to the second case. The signs are consistent with true drowning. The type of drowning is true, that is, aspiration. Which signs indicate this: Krushevsky's foam and subpleural spots. The blood sign is Casper's: the blood of the left heart is paler. Vitality is confirmed by diatoms, in the organs and bone marrow. As a sample, 1 l of water is taken from the water body.

Conclusion: type and main sign. General signs are not specific, so the set is assessed. In hanging there is an oblique furrow and signs of stretching. In ligature strangulation a horizontal furrow at the level of the cartilage. In manual strangulation bruises, nail marks and fracture of the cartilage. In true drowning pink foam, doughy lungs and diatoms. In compression asphyxia the main sign is the ecchymotic mask.

Review questions. The questions rest on the lesson slides and the content of the chapter. First: the definition of asphyxia and the types of mechanical asphyxia. Second: name the stages of the asphyxial period. Third: which of the general signs are relatively pathognomonic. Fourth: what is the difference between the furrow in hanging and in ligature strangulation. Fifth: the difference between true and asphyxial drowning and the significance of diatoms. Test yourself with these questions.
